question: In Sermon 2806, how does the woman described continue to acknowledge Jesus as Lord throughout his ministry and death?
answer: Spurgeon explains that the woman, even without a physical revelation of the divine, consistently calls Him "Lord" in every aspect of his work and suffering. She perceives Him as "a friend of publicans and sinners" and believes Him to be "the Son of the Highest." She also recognizes Him as "Lord of the sea who made the stormy waves lie still at His command" and as "the Master of diseases," before whom "all manner of sicknesses, and even devils, themselves, fled apace." Even in his crucifixion she salutes Him as Lord, echoing the dying thief’s prayer, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom." This continual acknowledgment underscores her unwavering confession of Christ’s lordship despite his humiliation and death. [Sermon 2806 — "Jesus Our Lord"]

She did so in the dying thief's prayer, "Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom." And she has done it thousands of times since.

question: Why does the passage say that the covenant is not between equals but between Lord and servant?
answer: The author of the work explains that the covenant is described as being between Lord and servant because it is fundamentally a covenant of God, who is the author and chief executor of it. As the passage states, "Now because this way of entring into covenant is not between those that are equall, but between Lord and servant," it emphasizes that the relationship is hierarchical, not reciprocal, and therefore properly termed a covenant of God rather than a human covenant. This distinction underscores the divine origin and authority of the covenant. [Ames — Marrow Of Sacred Divinity]

question: According to Dabney in his systematic theology, why is it impossible for Christ, as a finite nature, to possess infinite divine attributes?
answer: Dabney argues that attributing infinite endowments to a finite nature is logically impossible. He writes that “Even Omnipotence cannot make a part to contain the whole,” indicating that a created being, no matter how exalted, cannot contain the totality of divine power. Consequently, while divine works may be ascribed to Christ, the ascription must respect the clear limit between what finite, dependent power can achieve and what is beyond all created power. [Systematic — Dabney Systematic Theology]

question: How does the author of 'Vestiges of Creation' use fetal development to argue that man is a more advanced form of earlier animal orders?
answer: The author of *Vestiges of Creation* argues that the progressive stages of fetal growth demonstrate a continuity between lower and higher animal forms. He writes that "the human foetus, for example, assuming in succession the peculiarities of structure of the reptile, of the fish, of the bird, and of man." From this observation he concludes that man is merely a more perfectly developed reptile and that the various orders of animals differ only in the stage they occupy in this unfolding series of life. This reasoning is presented as part of his broader analogy that, just as physical laws shape the heavens, they likewise shape the development of life from simple to complex. [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol2]

question: According to Spurgeon in this sermon, what does Scripture say about the destiny of those who reject the Savior?
answer: Spurgeon teaches that the biblical text leaves no doubt that those who persist in sin and reject Christ will face everlasting punishment. He emphasizes that the Scripture plainly declares a future of both torment and blessing, stating, "there will be goats upon the left hand as well as sheep on the right, tares to be burned as well as wheat to be garnered, chaff to be blown away as well as corn to be preserved." He rejects the so‑called critical method that tries to dilute the phrase "all men" and insists that the Holy Ghost meant exactly what He wrote: all humanity will be judged according to their response to the Gospel. Consequently, Spurgeon affirms that there will be "a dreadful hell as well as a glorious heaven, and there is no decree to the contrary." [Sermon 1516 — "Salvation by Knowing the Truth"]

There will be a dreadful hell as well as a glorious heaven, and there is no decree to the contrary.

question: What proof does the passage give that the human soul itself bears witness to the existence of the true God?
answer: The passage argues that the soul, even while imprisoned in the body and weakened by lusts and passions, can recover its sober condition and then "calls God by this name [deus, not Jupiter, Apollo, etc.] because it is the proper name of the true God." In this sober state the soul naturally uses words like ‘Great God,’ ‘Good God,’ and ‘God grant,’ directing its thoughts upward toward heaven rather than to any earthly capital, thereby evidencing an innate awareness of a singular, true deity. The text further supports this by noting that even pagan philosophers such as Varro, cited by Augustine, recognized a monotheistic principle, stating that worship should be confined to one God. This convergence of internal soul testimony and external philosophical acknowledgment is presented as proof of divine existence. [Systematic — Shedd Dogmatic Theology Vol1]

question: What does the sermon say the phrase 'gird up the loins of your mind' means and why it is important?
answer: The sermon explains that the Apostle’s exhortation is a vivid metaphor: believers must 'gird up the loins of your mind' in order to bind the loose and flowing thoughts that act like unwieldy garments, preventing active spiritual exercise. As the passage notes, 'the garments of the Easterns... are long flowing robes and, unless the raiment is well gird about the wearer, there is little or nothing that he can do in the way of active exercise.' By tightening these mental encumbrances, Christians avoid laxity and become capable of diligent moral and spiritual work. [Sermon 2649 — "Girded for the Work"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2649 — "Girded for the Work"]
meta.passage:
What would God have me do as the result of receiving such teaching as this?" From what Peter had already said, like a true logician, he draws a wise inference and says, "Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the Grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ."

We shall only have time to consider the first few words of the Apostle's exhortation, "Therefore gird up the loins of your mind." And, concerning them, we will ask three questions, First, What are we to do? Secondly, Why are we to do it? And, thirdly, How are we to do it?

First, let us enquire, WHAT ARE WE TO DO? "Gird up the loins of your mind."

The metaphor used by Peter is a very simple one. The garments of the Easterns, as you know, are not like ours, but are long flowing robes and, unless the raiment is well gird about the wearer, there is little or nothing that he can do in the way of active exercise. In a spiritual sense, the injunction, "Gird up the loins of your mind," is a very proper one to be addressed to those of us who have various loose and flowing things which are almost as natural to us as garments are to the body. They must be gird about us very tightly or else they will become an encumbrance and a hindrance.

We may possibly understand what is meant by our text if we, first, consider the opposite condition. Some persons are notorious for their laxity--whatever they have about them is very loosely attached to them. I am grieved to say that there are some professing Christians who are very lax even in matters of morality.

question: What source of power does the passage claim will raise the dead, and how does it describe the differing experiences of the godly and the wicked?
answer: The work explains that the resurrection is effected solely 'by the power of Christ ; no power else can do it.' It rejects any natural ability to rise, citing Job xiv.14 and Psalm 49, and emphasizes that all will be raised by Christ’s power. However, the passage distinguishes the experiences: the godly will rise 'with boldness, joy, and ravishment,' whereas the wicked will rise 'with fear, shame, and astonishment.' This contrast underscores the necessity of relying on Christ’s mighty power for both comfort in this life and confidence at death. [Sibbes — Works Vol07]

meta.heading: [Sermon 2775 — "David Warned and Rewarded"]
meta.passage:
We have a Bible which is large enough to be a perfect library and which is also so compact that we can carry it about with us wherever we go! It is exactly the right size and it is just right in all other respects. It is just adapted to every individual in the world and it is also the most fit Book for any nation to use as an everyday guide as to its morals, its laws and its conduct in relation to both God and men.

There are two things mentioned in the text which made the Scriptures very dear to David. The first is that they had warned him against evil--"by them Your servant is warned." And the second is that obedience to the Scriptures had brought him a great reward--"and in keeping them there is great reward."

First, then, THE SCRIPTURES HAD WARNED DAVID AGAINST EVIL.

We are so dull and so foolish that unless we are taught of God the Holy Spirit, we really know nothing as we ought to know it. Yet we are so headstrong and so obstinate that if we are not Divinely checked, we run with heedless impetuosity into all manner of evil. We need to be goaded on to everything that is good, but we need to be held in with a tight rein, or we shall plunge into many things that are evil. Even when we do not willfully choose the wrong, we seem to run into it by a sort of natural tendency--and we find ourselves bogged down before we know where we are. If, however, the Scripture is made to be our constant companion and guide, we shall be saved from many mistakes into which, otherwise, we are sure to fall.

You not only know it as a seed, but you know the blessed flowers that have grown out of it because, in His Grace, He became poor that you might be rich. And, in taking of those riches which He has procured for you, you have not only drunk of His bitter soup, but you have drunk of the spiced wine of His pomegranate, so that you now know the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ by that which is the fruit and the outcome of it.

I think that the Apostle here meant that we also know the Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ through what He has done for us. We might have known, as a matter of fact, that Jesus was gracious, but we could not have seen it so as practically to know it if He, having been rich, had not become poor, that we, through His poverty, might be rich. The way the Apostle shows that Truth of God is just this. He was urging the Corinthian Christians to liberality. They were a far richer community than the Church at Philippi, but He tells them that the Churches of Macedonia, out of their poverty, had often been generous to the poor and he persuades these Corinthians, who were better off, not to be behind the Philippi-ans.

After Paul had quoted this example to them, he felt that he had a far stronger argument to fall back upon. He seemed to say, "How am I to know your Grace except by your works?

question: What was Archbishop Cranmer's motivation for urging Calvin and other reformers to convene a "Godly Synod"?
answer: Archbishop Cranmer, who held "liberal and enlightened views on the subject of Protestant Union," was motivated to urge Calvin and other leading reformers to convene a "Godly Synod" by his observation of the Romish Church's actions. He noted that the Romish Church had convoked her Council of Trent and was "vigorously endeavouring to regain what she had lost by infusing new vigour into her corrupt system." Cranmer questioned why Protestants should neglect a similar effort, specifically asking Calvin, "Shall we neglect to call together a Godly Synod for the Refutation of Error, and for Restoring and Propagating the Truth? They are, as I am informed, making Decrees respecting the Worship of the Host; wherefore we ought to leave no stone unturned, not only that we may guard others against this Idolatry, but also that we may ourselves come to an Agreement on The Sacrament." His aim was to refute error, propagate truth, guard against idolatry, and achieve agreement among Protestants, especially concerning the sacrament, in direct response to the Romish Church's decrees.

question: According to the passage, why can a man not embrace the Savior while 'hugging his sin'?
answer: Spurgeon teaches that a man cannot embrace the Savior while continuing in sin because "there is no Savior for the man who will not forsake his sin." Such an individual cannot be among the people who shall run to Christ, as it is impossible to run to Christ while persisting in a sinful way of life. The passage explains that "while he hugs his sin, he cannot embrace the Savior who hates sin with a perfect hatred." Therefore, any attempt to seek the Lord or call upon Him under these conditions would be in vain.

meta.heading: [Sermon 2797 — "The Need and Nature of Conversion"]
meta.passage:
Then there follows, in due order, the promise of a people to be saved. The Savior shall not come to the earth in vain. He shall call a people unto Himself and "nations" shall run to Him. Then, following the promise of a Savior and the declaration of the certainty that many shall be saved by Him, there comes in this loving invitation, "Seek you the Lord while He may be found, call you upon Him while He is near." Since He is to have a people who shall be His, forever, put in your claim to be among them! And since, as a Savior, He is near to you, call upon Him and He will hear your call!

This brings us to our text which is consistent with the rest of the Chapter even though some people think it is not. Here we are told, first, that the wicked must forsake his ways. There is no Savior for the man who will not forsake his sin. Such a man can never be among the people who shall run to Christ, for how can he run to Christ while he continues in the way of sin? Such a man shall seek the Lord in vain and call upon Him in vain, for, while he hugs his sin, he cannot embrace the Savior who hates sin with a perfect hatred. This is the theme upon which I am going to now speak and I want to do it in the spirit of the Master, of whom Malachi wrote, "For who may abide the day of His coming? And who shall stand when He appears?

question: According to Spurgeon, what is the spiritual condition of God's people before their deliverance, and what prevents them from freeing themselves?
answer: Spurgeon teaches that before their deliverance, God's people are in a state of spiritual slavery, typified by the Israelites in Egypt. He describes them as "slaves, engaged like Israel of old in labors that savor more of earthly than of heavenly things—brick-makers, building houses not for themselves, for they find no city to dwell in." They are "toiling and laboring here as unwilling servants, thinking, perhaps, they shall receive goodly wages, but they receive no wages, except the whip upon their shoulders." This condition applies even to God's people until they hear the "trumpet of jubilee" and are brought forth by divine power. They are unable to free themselves because they are "slaves to a power which we can never overcome by our own unassisted strength," much like the Israelites could not have rebelled against Pharaoh's overwhelming might.

meta.heading: [Sermon 322 — "A Divine Challenge!"]
meta.passage:
In fact, the Word which Jehovah is now speaking to the entire world with the solemn authority of an imperial mandate is this—"Thus says the Lord, let My people go, that they may serve Me."

It will be necessary in addressing you this evening, to recall to your minds the position which the Israelites held in Egypt. It is a type of the position of all the Lord's people before the Most High God, who with a high hand and an outstretched arm brings them out of their bondage. The people of the Lord are slaves. Though their names are in His book, yet they are slaves, engaged like Israel of old in labors that savor more of earthly than of heavenly things—brick-makers, building houses not for themselves, for they find no city to dwell in. They are toiling and laboring here as unwilling servants, thinking, perhaps, they shall receive goodly wages, but they receive no wages, except the whip upon their shoulders. Every man in his unrenewed state is a slave. Even God's people are slaves as well as others, till they hear the trumpet of jubilee and at the Word and by the power of God are brought forth out of the place of their slavery. We are slaves—slaves to a power which we can never overcome by our own unassisted strength. If all the inhabitants of Goshen—the Israelites, I mean—had concerted measures to rebel against Pharaoh and had said, "We will be free"—in but a few hours, the tremendous power of that great monarch of Egypt would have crushed out the last spark of hope.

question: What is the first point of information Flavel provides concerning Christ's establishment of order in the church?
answer: Flavel teaches that the first point of information, or "consectary," is that "Christ hath established an order and government in his house, which none must violate." He describes the church as "a well ordered family, or household, whereof Christ is the Head, Christians members, ministers stewards, the ordinances food to be dispensed by them in season." In this established order, everyone is to keep their proper place: pastors are to feed and govern, and people are to know, honor, and obey their leaders. Flavel emphasizes that this order is "the church's beauty," and the extent of Christ's presence is directly related to the observance of His rule and order within the church.

question: What significance does the repeated word 'Yet' have in this sermon passage?
answer: The sermon teaches that the repeated word "Yet" functions as a turning point from judgment to hope. It is described as "an ominous word as to the past!" and also as "a cheering word as to the future!" The passage stresses that although God's people have fallen into sin and despair, the utterance of "Yet" signals that God has not cast them away and that restoration is still possible. In this way, "Yet" conveys that despite the backsliding and sorrow, the promise of divine mercy endures. [Sermon 564 — "A Promise For Us And For Our Children"]

meta.heading: [Sermon 564 — "A Promise For Us And For Our Children"]
meta.passage:
Observe that the text begins with the word, "Yet." What an ominous word as to the past! What a cheering word as to the future! "Yet." "Yet." What black words are those which come before it? Surely all is not well. Look at the preceding verses and see. God's people were represented as being in a sadly backsliding state. They had lost their love to the service of God. They neglected His altar. They brought Him no thank offerings. No, they had fallen into a state of sin until they wearied God with their iniquity.

Consequently they fell into a condition of sorrow--God gave them up to the curse and the reproach. It may be that such is our case this morning, though we are God's people. Perhaps our soul lies cleaving in the dust. We have forgotten to run with diligence in the way of God's Commandments. We have fallen into a lukewarm state. We are following afar off. It may be that we have even fallen into sin and sitting in this House of Prayer we confess with Pharaoh's butler, "I do remember my faults this day."

It is very possible that we have been made too smart for our sins. God may have hidden His face from us. Our faith may be flagging--our graces may be withering. It will be so, it must be so when we forsake our God. If we leave the flowing Fountain to trust in broken cisterns, we shall soon know the bitterness of thirst. "Yet." "Yet," says the text--"yet," though you have fallen into this state, do not despair! Though you have transgressed very foully, do not think God has cast you away! "Yet now hear, O Jacob, My servant.
